nameStory: This beetle gets its "red-necked" name from the rusty-orange coloring on its thorax (the middle section behind its head), which contrasts beautifully with its darker body. The "false blister beetle" part comes from its resemblance to true blister beetles, which can secrete chemicals that cause skin blisters - but don't worry, this harmless impostor is all looks and no sting!
description: The Red-necked False Blister Beetle is a slender, medium-sized beetle that looks like it's wearing a rusty orange vest over a dark suit. These beetles grow to about half an inch long and have an elongated, somewhat flattened body shape. Adults are often seen on flowers during summer months, where they feed on pollen and nectar. Despite their intimidating family name, they're completely harmless plant-eaters that play an important role as pollinators.

idTips.label: Rusty orange thorax
idTips.description: The middle body section (thorax) is distinctly rusty-orange to reddish-brown, creating a striking collar effect against the darker head and wing covers

idTips.label: Dark wing covers
idTips.description: The hard wing covers (elytra) are dark brown to blackish, often with a slight metallic sheen when caught in sunlight

idTips.label: Slender build
idTips.description: Body feels lightweight and delicate if handled, with a notably narrow waist between the thorax and abdomen, unlike stockier beetles

idTips.label: Long antennae
idTips.description: Thread-like antennae extend well beyond the head, often nearly half the body length, and move actively when the beetle is disturbed

idTips.label: Flower-visiting behavior
idTips.description: Almost always found on or near flowers, moving deliberately among petals and often covered with a light dusting of pollen

habitat: Look for these beetles in sunny woodland edges, meadows, and gardens where wildflowers bloom abundantly. They're particularly fond of areas with goldenrod, asters, and other composite flowers, often in slightly disturbed habitats like old fields or forest clearings. In New England, they prefer elevations below 2,000 feet and seem most common in areas with well-drained soils.

seasonality.spring: Adults are just emerging and may be found on early blooming trees and shrubs, though they're not yet at peak activity.
seasonality.summer: Peak season for adult activity - easily spotted on a wide variety of flowers from June through August, most active during warm, sunny afternoons.
seasonality.fall: Still active into September on late-season flowers like goldenrod and asters, but numbers decline as temperatures drop.
seasonality.winter: Adults have died off, and the species overwinters as larvae in decaying wood or plant material underground.

funFact: Despite being called "false" blister beetles, these insects are actually more effective pollinators than many of the "real" blister beetles they mimic - nature's version of the student becoming better than the teacher!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with true blister beetles, but those tend to have more uniform coloring and can actually cause skin irritation if handled roughly. Remember: "Red neck, you're safe to check" - the distinctive orange thorax is your clue that this is the harmless false version.
contextualKnowledge: The "false" in their name reflects an old classification confusion where these beetles were grouped with true blister beetles due to similar appearance, but they're actually in a completely different family with very different chemistry and behavior. This is a great example of how looks can be deceiving in the insect world!
compareHints: Since this is the only Ischnomera species commonly found in New England, compare it with other false blister beetles in the region, which typically lack the distinctive rusty-orange thorax coloring. Most other family members are more uniformly colored in browns or blacks, making the Red-necked False Blister Beetle the fashionable standout of its group.
